Reparametrizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Palette-based Color and Luminance Editing

Conference: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers; December 01–04, 2026; Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaSIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers (SA Conference Papers ’26), December 01–04, 2026, Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaDOI: 10.1145/3829340.3842202ISBN: 979-8-4007-2842-6/2026/12CCS: Computing methodologies RenderingCCS: Computing methodologies Image processing
Cheng-Kang Ted Chao email: cchao8@gmu.edu Affiliation: George Mason University, USA and Yotam Gingold email: ygingold@gmu.edu Affiliation: George Mason University, USA
© cc
Abstract.

Professional color editing requires precise control over both color (hue and saturation) and lightness, ideally through separate, independent controls. We present a real-time interactive color editing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that supports palette-based recoloring, per-palette tone curves for color-aware luminance adjustment, and pixel-level color constraints. Rather than training a new representation from scratch, we reparameterize the spherical harmonics of a pretrained vanilla 3DGS to encode view-dependent palette weights. We simultaneously solve for weights and palette colors via a loss based on image-space sparsity. Luminance editing is realized as a per-pixel weight shift along the achromatic axis, which we show is equivalent to a per-pixel palette-aware luminance edit. This view-space formulation addresses a core limitation of prior primitive-space methods, where alpha-blending breaks per-Gaussian sparsity and causes edits to bleed into unintended regions. Our edits run in tens of milliseconds via an iteratively reweighted least squares and damped block-coordinate descent that couples tone curves and palette shifts under view-space sparsity. Our representation can be efficiently baked back into a vanilla 3DGS, preserving compatibility with standard viewers. We demonstrate sparser, more localized edits than prior palette-based 3DGS methods, while enabling independent luminance control per palette color and view-consistent pixel-level constraints, capabilities previously unavailable for 3DGS.

Keywords: 
3D gaussian splatting, palette-based image editing, color, optimization, luminance, tone curves

1. Introduction

Color grading for 3D scenes is central to modern content creation, from visual effects and film production (Debevec, 2008) to virtual production and augmented reality (Jeffrey Okun and Susan Zwerman, 2020). Beyond global adjustments, artists need selective control over specific color ranges, with edits that remain photorealistic and geometrically consistent across viewpoints. In 2D, palette-based editing (Chang et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2018) offers an intuitive workflow by expressing each pixel as a mixture of a small set of palette colors and propagating edits by keeping the mixing weights fixed. This paradigm has been improved through better palette extraction and sparser, more localized decompositions (Aksoy et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019; Chao et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2025b). Professional workflows benefit from independent lightness control per color range, e.g., via palette-aware tone curves (Chao et al., 2023a). Extending these capabilities to 3D scenes requires not only multi-view consistency, but also palette decompositions that remain sparse and editable in the rendered images users observe and edit.

Recent reconstruction methods such as NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2021) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) enable photorealistic novel-view synthesis, and several methods adapt palette-based editing to NeRF (Kuang et al., 2023; Gong et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022) and 3DGS (Ren et al., 2024; Bi et al., 2025) by decomposing each primitive’s diffuse color into weighted combinations of palette colors. However, primitive-level decomposition suffers from a fundamental mismatch: alpha-blending many Gaussians at a single pixel breaks per-primitive sparsity, producing dense pixel-level decompositions that cause palette edits to bleed into unintended regions (Fig. 9). Palette-based NeRF methods face similar issues and additionally require expensive preprocessing for weight guidance. Prior palette-based 3DGS methods also lack color-aware tone curves, and their pixel-level color constraints require joint re-optimization of palette and view-dependent components, preventing real-time interaction (see Fig. 6 in supplemental)

We present a real-time color grading framework for 3DGS that resolves these limitations by finetuning a pretrained vanilla 3DGS into a palette subspace, where each Gaussian’s spherical harmonics (SH) encode view-dependent palette weights instead of RGB colors. Palette decomposition then occurs at the pixel-level after splatting, in the same view-space where edits are perceived and specified. To absorb the storage overhead, we factorize the higher-order weight SH into rank-1 form with little quality loss (Table 1). This view-space formulation supports three complementary editing controls (Fig. 1, 2, and 8): direct palette manipulation, per-palette tone curves for color-aware luminance adjustment, and pixel-level color constraints from any rendered view. To ensure perceptually similar colors receive similar decompositions, we introduce a color consistency loss based on inverse barycentric coordinates with respect to the current palette. We adapt the 2D constraint-driven solver of Chao et al. (2023a) via iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) and damped block-coordinate descent (dBCD) that couples tone curves and palette shifts, running in tens of milliseconds per edit. Edits bake back into a vanilla 3DGS at essentially no cost for palette edits, or with a brief finetuning step (a few seconds) for luminance edits, preserving compatibility with standard viewers. We evaluate on multiple scenes and show that our framework provides editing capabilities unavailable in prior palette-based 3DGS methods while also improving edit quality and interactivity. Code for this work can be found at https://github.com/tedchao/ReparamGS-Palette.

2. Related Work

Appearance editing in neural scene representations.

Neural scene representations such as NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2021) and 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023) have enabled a wide range of appearance editing techniques by explicitly modeling view-dependent radiance. Text-driven editing (Haque et al., 2023; Zhuang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Kamata et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2023) and neural style transfer (Zhang et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025a) support semantic or artistic modifications but lack direct color control and often struggle with multi-view consistency, making them unsuitable for professional color grading. Relighting and tone mapping methods (Gao et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) target photometric consistency through physically based rendering or luminance-domain processing, but offer no palette-based abstractions or selective color control. Segmentation-driven editing methods (Cen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025; Tsang et al., 2026; Rutayisire et al., 2025; Mazzucchelli et al., 2026) support object- or region-level recoloring, and intrinsic decomposition methods (Lanvin et al., 2026) enable material-level edits via per-pixel reflectance-shading separation. These approaches decompose scenes by spatial regions or material components rather than by color, targeting a different class of edits: they do not provide per-color tone-curve control, color-coherent propagation across spatially disconnected regions, or interactive constraint-driven optimization. They are orthogonal to our palette-based formulation.

Closer to our work, Tojo and Umetani (2022) extends posterization-style editing (Chao et al., 2021) to NeRFs for synthetic scenes, while PaletteNeRF (Kuang et al., 2023) and RecolorNeRF (Gong et al., 2023) support real-world scenes via palette decomposition of volumetric points, at the cost of expensive preprocessing and slow rendering. Recent palette-based 3DGS methods (Ren et al., 2024; Bi et al., 2025) achieve real-time performance by decomposing each Gaussian’s color into mixtures of global palette colors, but their primitive-level decomposition does not survive alpha-blending: sparsity at the primitive level does not translate into sparsity in the rendered image, manifesting as color bleeding (Fig. 5 in supplemental). We address this limitation by reparametrizing a pretrained 3DGS into a palette subspace where decomposition occurs at the pixel level after splatting, while remaining compatible with standard 3DGS viewers via bake-back.

Palette-based image recoloring.

Palette-based image recoloring enables intuitive color control by representing each pixel as a mixture of a small set of representative palette colors. Chang et al. (2015) introduced this paradigm via color clustering and radial-basis-function-weighted color deformation. Subsequent work formulated palette extraction and decomposition geometrically in color space: Tan et al. (2016) proposed convex-hull-based decomposition into translucent color layers, and Tan et al. (2018) extended this to spatially coherent additive mixing weights in RGBXY-space, enabling recoloring and color harmonization (Tan et al., 2025). Other approaches improve palette quality via optimization (Wang et al., 2019) or coarse-to-fine convex hull construction (Sun et al., 2023). Continuous palette formulations (Shugrina et al., 2020) provide an alternative to discrete palettes for direct manipulation of color distributions. Independent of palette extraction, Chao et al. (2023a) introduced palette-aware tone curves to support independent lightness and contrast control per palette color and image-space color constraints. Extensions to video recoloring compute temporally coherent RGBT palettes (Du et al., 2021), with later work accelerating palette evolution via Bézier interpolation between frames (Du et al., 2025). A fundamental limitation of palette-based recoloring is its difficulty in selectively editing objects that share similar colors, addressed by incorporating segmentation (Chao et al., 2023b) or by extracting semantic palettes in high-dimensional feature spaces (Du et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). Unmixing approaches (Aksoy et al., 2016; Aksoy et al., 2017; Koyama and Goto, 2018) instead formulate recoloring as energy minimization to produce sparse layers of nearly homogeneous colors. All these methods operate in image space, where palette weights are defined, regularized, and edited at the pixel-level; this assumption breaks down for 3D scenes (Fig. 4 in supplemental), motivating our view-space formulation.

3. Background and Motivation

Recent work (Ren et al., 2024; Bi et al., 2025) extends 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023) to palette-based color editing by decomposing each Gaussian’s diffuse color as a linear combination of a small set of palette colors. Let KK denote the number of palette colors, 𝐏∈ℝK×3\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 3} a trainable global palette shared across the scene, and 𝐰i∈ℝK\mathbf{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} a per-Gaussian weight vector with wi,k∈[0,1]w_{i,k}\in[0,1] and ∑kwi,k=1\sum_{k}w_{i,k}=1. Gaussian ii’s diffuse component is then 𝐜id=𝐰i⊤​𝐏\mathbf{c}_{i}^{d}=\mathbf{w}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{P}, and view-dependent effects are captured by an additive specular component 𝐜is​(θ,ϕ)\mathbf{c}_{i}^{s}(\theta,\phi) at viewpoint (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi), modeled via low-order spherical harmonics (Ren et al., 2024) or neural offsets (Bi et al., 2025), yielding the full per-Gaussian color 𝐜i​(θ,ϕ)=𝐜id+𝐜is​(θ,ϕ)\mathbf{c}_{i}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbf{c}_{i}^{d}+\mathbf{c}_{i}^{s}(\theta,\phi). Weights 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} are stored per-Gaussian or, for compression, decoded from each Gaussian’s position through a small Hash-MLP (Müller et al., 2022), and jointly optimized with 𝐏\mathbf{P} and the Gaussian parameters under sparsity regularization (Aksoy et al., 2017). Letting 𝒩𝐱\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{x}} denote the depth-sorted set of Gaussians affecting pixel 𝐱\mathbf{x} and αi′\alpha_{i}^{\prime} each Gaussian’s opacity modulated by its 2D spatial footprint, plugging the diffuse decomposition into the 3DGS rendering pipeline (Kerbl et al., 2023) and factoring out 𝐏\mathbf{P} gives:

(1) 𝐂(𝐱;θ,ϕ)=[∑i∈𝒩𝐱𝐰i⊤​αi′​∏j=1i−1(1−αj′)]​𝐏⏟diffuse: weighted palette+∑i∈𝒩𝐱𝐜is​(θ,ϕ)​αi′​∏j=1i−1(1−αj′)⏟specular.\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=\underbrace{\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{x}}}\mathbf{w}_{i}^{\top}\,\alpha_{i}^{\prime}\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha_{j}^{\prime})\right]\mathbf{P}}_{\text{diffuse: weighted palette}}+\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{x}}}\mathbf{c}_{i}^{s}(\theta,\phi)\,\alpha_{i}^{\prime}\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha_{j}^{\prime})}_{\text{specular}}.

This formulation reveals two fundamental limitations of primitive-space decomposition. First, the pixel-level palette weights (first term of Eq. 1) are alpha-blended per-Gaussian weights 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i}. Even when each 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} is sparse and sums to one, blending many Gaussians at a pixel breaks sparsity, producing nonzero weights across most palette colors and causing edits to bleed into unintended regions (Fig. 9, and supplemental). In regions of sparse coverage, the residual (1−∑jwj)(1-\sum_{j}w_{j}) contributes black, diluting editing control. Second, because 𝐏\mathbf{P} affects only the diffuse term while specular highlights remain independent, enforcing pixel-level color constraints is ill-posed: optimizing the palette alone causes bleeding; adding regularization still bleeds, converges slowly (over 10 seconds on GPU), and drives the palette to extreme values; jointly optimizing the palette and specular SH converges faster but shows severe bleeds, as SH encode global view-dependent effects with no clear strategy to impose local regularization (see Fig. 6 in supplemental).

4. Method: Representation and Finetuning

Our goal is to enable real-time, high-quality palette-based editing of 3DGS scenes through three controls: direct palette manipulation, per-palette tone curves for independent luminance adjustment, and pixel-level color constraints that propagate consistently across novel views (Figs. 1 and 8). This requires two design choices. First, since edits are specified and perceived at the pixel-level, we splat palette weights rather than colors (§4.1) and regularize them in view-space for sparsity and color consistency (§4.2). Second, to remain compatible with vanilla 3DGS, we reparametrize a pretrained vanilla 3DGS by freezing geometric parameters and replacing the color SH with palette-weight SH, jointly optimized with the palette (§4.3). This keeps the palette linear in the rendering pipeline, enabling closed-form bake-back for palette edits and a brief finetuning step for tone-curve edits. An overview of our method is shown in Fig. 3. Editing is deferred to §5.

4.1. View-space Palette Decomposition

We work entirely in RGB-space throughout the framework. Given a pretrained vanilla 3DGS, we fix all geometric parameters (position 𝝁i\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}, covariance 𝚺i\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}, opacity αi\alpha_{i}) and finetune11 1 Although the SH coefficients are randomly initialized, we refer to this stage as finetuning because it adapts the pretrained Gaussian geometry to a new appearance representation rather than training a 3DGS from scratch. only the per-Gaussian SH coefficients to encode view-dependent palette weights 𝐰i∈ℝK\mathbf{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} instead of RGB colors, where KK is the total number of palette colors. (2) 𝐖⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)=∑i∈𝒩𝐱βi​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)​𝐰i​(θ,ϕ),\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{x}}}\beta_{i}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\,\mathbf{w}_{i}(\theta,\phi),

4.2. Barycentric Supervision

The view-space weights of §4.1 are directly available for regularization, but two further properties are critical for high-quality palette editing: sparsity, which prevents edits from bleeding across colors, and color consistency, which ensures similar colors propagate edits identically (Fig. 6 in supplemental). We achieve both properties simultaneously by supervising the splatted weights 𝐖⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi) against the barycentric decomposition of the frozen splatted color 𝐜⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)∈ℝ3\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\in\mathbb{R}^{3} of the vanilla 3DGS over the current palette 𝐏\mathbf{P}: barycentric coordinates are inherently 4-sparse for any color inside a tetrahedral wedge, and similar colors lying within the same wedge receive nearby barycentric coordinates by construction.

To realize this barycentric decomposition, we tessellate 𝐏\mathbf{P} into K−2K-2 tetrahedral wedges Ti=(𝟎,𝟏,𝐩i,𝐩i+1)T_{i}=(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1},\mathbf{p}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{i+1}), i=1,…,K−2i=1,\ldots,K-2 with wraparound on i+1i+1, each fanning around the line of greys (Tan et al., 2018). Choosing which wedge a given color belongs to requires the chromatic vertices to be ordered around the grey axis, and re-sorting them after every gradient step would break the optimization. We sidestep this by parameterizing each chromatic vertex 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} in HSL-space with hue hi∈[0,2​π)h_{i}\in[0,2\pi), saturation si∈[0,1]s_{i}\in[0,1], and lightness li∈[0,1]l_{i}\in[0,1], recovering its RGB position via the standard HSL-to-RGB transform. Hues are represented as cumulative offsets from a learnable base angle h0h_{0}: hi=(h0+∑k<igk)mod2​πh_{i}=(h_{0}+\sum_{k<i}g_{k})\bmod 2\pi, where the gaps gk=2​π⋅softplus⁡(g~k)/∑jsoftplus⁡(g~j)g_{k}=2\pi\cdot\mathrm{softplus}(\tilde{g}_{k})/\sum_{j}\mathrm{softplus}(\tilde{g}_{j}) are softplus-normalized to sum to 2​π2\pi, so the 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} are always in counter-clockwise hue order around the achromatic axis without explicit sorting.

With the wedge tessellation well-defined throughout optimization, we construct target barycentric coordinates 𝐖bary​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)∈ℝK\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{bary}}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} that decompose 𝐜⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi) over 𝐏\mathbf{P}. A 2D illustration of the algorithm can be seen in Fig. 4. For each wedge TiT_{i}, we solve a 3×33\times 3 linear system to obtain the unique barycentric coordinates (ai,bi,ci,di)(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i},d_{i}) satisfying 𝐜=ai​𝟎+bi​𝟏+ci​𝐩i+di​𝐩i+1\mathbf{c}=a_{i}\mathbf{0}+b_{i}\mathbf{1}+c_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}+d_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i+1} and ai+bi+ci+di=1a_{i}+b_{i}+c_{i}+d_{i}=1. 4.3. Joint Palette and Weight SH Finetuning

We finetune the per-Gaussian SH coefficients {fl,m,iw}\{f^{w}_{l,m,i}\} and palette parameters {h0,g~k,si,li}\{h_{0},\tilde{g}_{k},s_{i},l_{i}\} jointly against the barycentric targets, minimizing ℒ=ℒcolor+λpos​ℒpos+λcompact​ℒcompact+λsep​ℒsep\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{color}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pos}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pos}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{compact}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{compact}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}, where ℒcolor=1H​W​∑𝐱‖𝐖⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)−𝐖bary​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)‖22\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{color}}=\frac{1}{HW}\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\|\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)-\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{bary}}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\|_{2}^{2} is the barycentric supervision loss (§ 4.2). The auxiliary terms regularize the splatted weights and the palette geometry: ℒpos=mean⁡(ReLU⁡(−𝐖))\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pos}}=\mathrm{mean}(\mathrm{ReLU}(-\mathbf{W})) discourages negative splatted weights without breaking the linearity of the SH-to-weights map required for closed-form bake-back; ℒcompact=∑i=1K−2vol⁡(Ti)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{compact}}=\sum_{i=1}^{K-2}\mathrm{vol}(T_{i}) is the sum of wedge volumes, counterbalancing ℒcolor\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{color}}’s tendency to create non-representative palette; and ℒsep\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}} penalizes any hue gap gkg_{k} falling below a minimum fraction of the even spacing 2​π/(K−2)2\pi/(K-2), preventing palette from collapsing. We schedule λcompact\lambda_{\mathrm{compact}} so that compactness pressure ramps up in the late stage of training, allowing the palette to first expand toward the scene’s color distribution before being tightened. Full hyperparameter values, the schedule, and additional implementation details are provided in §6.

4.4. Rank-1 Factorization of Higher-Order Weight SH

The representation in §4.1 replaces each Gaussian’s color SH with KK-channel weight SH, blowing up per-Gaussian SH storage by a factor of K/3K/3 relative to vanilla 3DGS (2×2\times for K=6K=6). To mitigate this, we factorize the higher-order (l≥1l\geq 1) weight SH coefficients via a reshaped outer product, leaving the band-zero (l=0l=0) term unfactorized. Empirically, this gives negligible reconstruction loss compared to finetuning with the full weight SH (Table 1) and produces visually comparable recoloring results, though not pixel-identical (Fig. 5). This holds even on highly reflective, view-dependent content, where the factorization preserves specular highlights with little quality loss at lower memory (Fig. 6). To describe the factorization, we first fix notation for the unfactorized form. Let LL denote the maximum SH band; each Gaussian ii has (L+1)2−1(L+1)^{2}-1 higher-order SH coefficients per channel, and stacking all KK channels gives a matrix 𝐌i∈ℝK×((L+1)2−1)\mathbf{M}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times((L+1)^{2}-1)}. The view-dependent weight vector at direction (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) is

(3) 𝐰i​(θ,ϕ)=𝐟iw,0+𝐌i​𝐘≥1​(θ,ϕ),\mathbf{w}_{i}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbf{f}^{w,0}_{i}+\mathbf{M}_{i}\,\mathbf{Y}^{\geq 1}(\theta,\phi),

where 𝐟iw,0∈ℝK\mathbf{f}^{w,0}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} holds the band-zero coefficients and 𝐘≥1​(θ,ϕ)∈ℝ(L+1)2−1\mathbf{Y}^{\geq 1}(\theta,\phi)\in\mathbb{R}^{(L+1)^{2}-1} are the higher-order SH basis values. To factorize, choose positive integers P,Q≥1P,Q\geq 1 with P⋅Q=K⋅((L+1)2−1)P\cdot Q=K\cdot((L+1)^{2}-1) and store 𝐚i∈ℝP\mathbf{a}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{P}, 𝐛i∈ℝQ\mathbf{b}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{Q} per Gaussian. We form 𝐒i=vec⁡(𝐚i​𝐛i⊤)∈ℝP​Q\mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{b}_{i}^{\top})\in\mathbb{R}^{PQ} via row-major vectorization, and reshape it into the approximated coefficient matrix 𝐌^i∈ℝK×((L+1)2−1)\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times((L+1)^{2}-1)} by

(4) 𝐌^i​[k,l​m]=𝐒i​[l​m⋅K+k],\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{i}[k,lm]=\mathbf{S}_{i}[lm\cdot K+k],

for 0≤k<K0\leq k<K and 0≤l​m<(L+1)2−10\leq lm<(L+1)^{2}-1, so successive KK-chunks of 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i} fill the columns of 𝐌^i\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{i}. The approximated weight vector follows Eq. 3 with 𝐌i\mathbf{M}_{i} replaced by 𝐌^i\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{i}. Note that 𝐚i​𝐛i⊤\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{b}_{i}^{\top} is rank-1 but 𝐌^i\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{i} in general is not. This reduces per-Gaussian SH storage from K⋅(L+1)2K\cdot(L+1)^{2} to K+P+QK+P+Q. By AM-GM, P+QP+Q is minimized at P=QP=Q subject to P⋅Q=K⋅((L+1)2−1)P\cdot Q=K\cdot((L+1)^{2}-1). For K=6K=6, L=3L=3, the closest integer factorization is (P,Q)=(9,10)(P,Q)=(9,10), giving 2525 scalars per Gaussian, roughly half of vanilla 3DGS’s 4848 (Table 1).

5. Method: Editing

With the palette and per-Gaussian weight SH finetuned (§4), users edit the scene in real-time via three constraint types: pixel-level color constraints (clicking a point in any rendered view and choosing a target color), palette constraints (modifying a palette), or per-palette tone-curve constraints (placing control points on a curve). All three feed a single optimization that seeks the smallest change to the palette and tone curves satisfying all constraints simultaneously, leaving the splatted weights and Gaussian parameters fixed. We define the editing model and constraint types (§5.1), then describe a constraint-driven solver based on iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) and damped block coordinate descent (dBCD) (§5.2).

5.1. Editing Model and Constraints

Let 𝐏∈ℝK×3\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 3} denote the trained palette and 𝐖⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)∈ℝK\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} the splatted weights at pixel 𝐱\mathbf{x} from viewpoint (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi). We associate each palette vertex 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} with a tone curve fi:[0,1]→[0,1]f_{i}:[0,1]\to[0,1] defined as a biharmonic function (Chao et al., 2023a) parametrized by user-placed control points; initially every fif_{i} is an identity function and the palette is unchanged. We discretize each fif_{i} at SS equally spaced sample points and let 𝐋i∈ℝS\mathbf{L}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} denote the vector of sampled values. The free editing variables are the palette modification Δ​𝐏∈ℝK×3\Delta\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 3} and the tone-curve sample vectors {𝐋i}i=1K\{\mathbf{L}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}, with all other parameters of the trained representation held fixed.

These two sets of variables determine the edited color at every pixel. We realize luminance editing by redistributing weight mass between the black (𝟘\mathbb{0}) and white (𝟙\mathbb{1}) palette of 𝐖\mathbf{W}. Concretely, given a viewpoint (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) and a pixel 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the splatted weights are 𝐖⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)=(W1,W2,W3,…,WK)\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=(W_{1},W_{2},W_{3},\ldots,W_{K}) with index 11 for black and index 22 for white, and the edited weights are (dropping the (𝐱,θ,ϕ)(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi) for compactness)

(5) W1′=W1−δ,W2′=W2+δ,Wi′=Wi​for​i≥3,W_{1}^{\prime}=W_{1}-\delta,\qquad W_{2}^{\prime}=W_{2}+\delta,\qquad W_{i}^{\prime}=W_{i}\;\;\text{for}\;\;i\geq 3,

where the luminance shift δ⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)\delta(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi) is computed from the per-pixel luminance L0​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)=𝐰L⊤​𝐂0​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)L_{0}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=\mathbf{w}_{L}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{0}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi) (BT.709 (International Telecommunication Union, 2015), 𝐰L=(0.2126,0.7152,0.0722)⊤\mathbf{w}_{L}=(0.2126,0.7152,0.0722)^{\top}, with 𝐂0\mathbf{C}_{0} the original rendered color) and the tone-curve samples as

(6) δ⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)=∑i=1KW~i​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)⋅(fi​(L0​(𝐱,θ,ϕ))−L0​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)),\delta(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\widetilde{W}_{i}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\cdot\big(f_{i}(L_{0}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi))-L_{0}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\big),

Here W~i\widetilde{W}_{i} is obtained by scaling the black and white entries of 𝐖\mathbf{W} by a small factor (we use η=0.01\eta=0.01) and renormalizing the result to sum to one, so chromatic palette colors dominate the shift. The edited color then follows from the modified weights and the edited palette is,

(7) 𝐂′​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)=(𝐏+Δ​𝐏)⊤​𝐖′​(𝐱,θ,ϕ).\mathbf{C}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=(\mathbf{P}+\Delta\mathbf{P})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi).

We prove in the supplemental materials that the weight shift alone (Eq. 5, with Δ​𝐏=𝟎\Delta\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{0}) is equivalent to a per-pixel luminance edit applied in proportion to each palette color’s chromatic weight: the resulting per-pixel BT.709 luminance is the chromatic-weight-blended target L0′​(𝐱)=∑i≥3W~i​fi​(L0​(𝐱))L_{0}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i\geq 3}\widetilde{W}_{i}\,f_{i}(L_{0}(\mathbf{x})), and the chromatic component of the rendered color is preserved exactly. When black and white are kept fixed (Δ​𝐏1=Δ​𝐏2=𝟎\Delta\mathbf{P}_{1}=\Delta\mathbf{P}_{2}=\mathbf{0}), Eq. 7 simplifies to

(8) 𝐂′​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)=(𝐏+Δ​𝐏)⊤​𝐖​(𝐱,θ,ϕ)+δ⁡(𝐱,θ,ϕ)​𝟙\mathbf{C}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)=(\mathbf{P}+\Delta\mathbf{P})^{\top}\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)+\delta(\mathbf{x};\theta,\phi)\mathbb{1}

Given this editing model, users specify the desired edit via three types of constraints. A pixel-level color constraint is a tuple (𝐱n,(θn,ϕn),𝐜ntgt)(\mathbf{x}_{n},\allowbreak(\theta_{n},\phi_{n}),\allowbreak\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}}) specifying that the edited color 𝐂′​(𝐱n,θn,ϕn)\mathbf{C}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta_{n},\phi_{n}), evaluated using the splatted weights 𝐖⁡(𝐱n,θn,ϕn)\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta_{n},\phi_{n}) at that pixel 𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{n}, should equal a target color 𝐜ntgt\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}}. A palette constraint is a pair (i,𝐩itgt)(i,\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}) specifying that the edited vertex 𝐩i+Δ​𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}+\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i} should equal 𝐩itgt\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}. A tone-curve constraint is a tuple (i,xn,yn)(i,x_{n},y_{n}) specifying that fi​(xn)=ynf_{i}(x_{n})=y_{n}, i.e., the user has placed a control point at (xn,yn)(x_{n},y_{n}) on the tone curve of palette color ii.

5.2. Constraint-Driven Solver

Given NimgN_{\mathrm{img}} pixel-level color constraints, NpN_{p} palette constraints, and NlN_{l} tone-curve constraints, our goal is to find the smallest change to Δ​𝐏∈ℝK×3\Delta\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 3} and {𝐋i∈ℝS}i=1K\{\mathbf{L}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{S}\}_{i=1}^{K} that satisfies all of them. We use 𝐁∈ℝS×S\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times S} to denote the discrete Laplacian with mirroring at endpoints for natural boundary conditions. The editing problem is a sparsity-regularized constrained optimization22 2 We use weq=103w_{\mathrm{eq}}=10^{3} to enforce constraints stiffly and wsp=0.1w_{\mathrm{sp}}=0.1.:

(9) min{𝐋i},Δ​𝐏Esp+weq​(Eimg+El+Ep),\min_{\{\mathbf{L}_{i}\},\,\Delta\mathbf{P}}\quad E_{\mathrm{sp}}\;+\;w_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\big(E_{\mathrm{img}}+E_{l}+E_{p}\big),

subject to 𝐋i,1=0\mathbf{L}_{i,1}=0 and 𝐋i,S=1\mathbf{L}_{i,S}=1 for all ii (pinning the first and last samples of each tone curve to 00 and 11), where EspE_{\mathrm{sp}} is the L2,1L_{2,1} sparsity term (Chao et al., 2023a):

(10) Esp=∑i=1K𝐋i⊤​𝐁⊤​𝐁​𝐋i+wsp⋅‖Δ​𝐩i‖22,E_{\mathrm{sp}}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sqrt{\,\mathbf{L}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{L}_{i}\;+\;w_{\mathrm{sp}}\cdot\|\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\,},

which induces global sparsity across palette colors and per-palette tone curves. The pixel-level color constraint loss EimgE_{\mathrm{img}} aggregates the squared color residual at every constraint pixel,

(11) Eimg=∑n=1Nimg‖𝐂′​(𝐱n,θn,ϕn)−𝐜ntgt‖22,E_{\mathrm{img}}\;=\;\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{img}}}\big\|\mathbf{C}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta_{n},\phi_{n})-\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}}\big\|_{2}^{2},

with 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime} from Eq. 7. The tone-curve and palette constraint losses are the squared discrepancies against their targets,

(12) El=∑i=1K‖𝐒i⊙𝐋i−𝐋itgt‖22,Ep=∑i∈Pc‖(𝐩i+Δ​𝐩i)−𝐩itgt‖22,E_{l}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{K}\|\mathbf{S}_{i}\odot\mathbf{L}_{i}-\mathbf{L}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad E_{p}\;=\;\sum_{i\in P_{c}}\big\|(\mathbf{p}_{i}+\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i})-\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}\big\|_{2}^{2},

where 𝐒i,𝐋itgt∈ℝS\mathbf{S}_{i},\mathbf{L}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} are selection/target vectors over curve ii’s sample positions, and PcP_{c} is the index set of constrained palette colors. User constraints on black and white (i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}) bypass EpE_{p} and directly update 𝐏\mathbf{P}, preserving the weight-shift equivalence (Eq. 8).

Our EimgE_{\mathrm{img}} couples the luminance and palette blocks in RGB-space: both tone curve contributions (via δ⁡(𝐱)⋅𝟙\delta(\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbb{1} in Eq. 8) and palette shifts (via ∑iWi​(𝐱)​Δ​𝐩i\sum_{i}W_{i}(\mathbf{x})\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}) contribute to the same color residual, and chromatic palette edits can produce nonzero projections onto the grey axis. Chao et al. (2023a) avoid this coupling by working in Lab-space, where tone curves affect only L∗L^{*} and palette shifts only a​bab, so the EimgE_{\mathrm{img}} residual separates along these axes. This orthogonality lets them apply BCD on lightness and chroma as independent sub-problems, yielding a fast solver. We thoroughly investigated a Lab-space formulation (supplemental), but adopting it requires a non-linear Lab-to-RGB map at edit time and breaks closed-form bake-back for palette edits. We therefore stay in RGB-space and design a tailored solver that exploits two structural properties of the problem.

A direct general-purpose solver would run far too slowly for interaction, because of the problem size: Eq. 9 has S​K+3​(K−2)SK+3(K-2) unknowns (e.g., ∼600{\sim}600 for S=100S=100, K=6K=6). The first property comes from the L2,1L_{2,1} square root in EspE_{\mathrm{sp}} (Eq. 10). Let ai=𝐋i⊤​𝐁⊤​𝐁​𝐋i+wsp​‖Δ​𝐩i‖22a_{i}=\mathbf{L}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{L}_{i}+w_{\mathrm{sp}}\|\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}\|_{2}^{2} denote the argument of the ii-th square root, so Esp=∑iaiE_{\mathrm{sp}}=\sum_{i}\sqrt{a_{i}}. The square root is non-differentiable at ai=0a_{i}=0 and produces a ai\sqrt{a_{i}}-denominator in the gradient, making the sub-problem in (𝐋,Δ​𝐏)(\mathbf{L},\Delta\mathbf{P}) non-linear. We sidestep both issues via the variational identity

(13) ai=mindi>0⁡ai2​di+di2,which has unique minimizer ​di∗=ai.\sqrt{a_{i}}\;=\;\min_{d_{i}>0}\,\frac{a_{i}}{2d_{i}}+\frac{d_{i}}{2},\>\text{which has unique minimizer }d_{i}^{*}=\sqrt{a_{i}}.

Introducing auxiliary scalars {di}i=1K\{d_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} and replacing EspE_{\mathrm{sp}} with the augmented energy E~sp​(𝐋,Δ​𝐏,{di})=∑i[ai2​di+di2]\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathbf{L},\Delta\mathbf{P},\{d_{i}\})=\sum_{i}\big[\tfrac{a_{i}}{2d_{i}}+\tfrac{d_{i}}{2}\big] preserves the minimum but makes the (𝐋,Δ​𝐏)(\mathbf{L},\Delta\mathbf{P}) block quadratic when {di}\{d_{i}\} are frozen. IRLS alternates between solving for (𝐋,Δ​𝐏)(\mathbf{L},\Delta\mathbf{P}) via a linear system with {di}\{d_{i}\} frozen and updating each di←aid_{i}\leftarrow\sqrt{a_{i}} in closed-form ({1/di}\{1/d_{i}\} serve as the IRLS weights). The second property targets the coupling: 𝐂′​(𝐱)\mathbf{C}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}) is affine in (𝐋,Δ​𝐏)(\mathbf{L},\Delta\mathbf{P}) jointly (Eq. 8), so EimgE_{\mathrm{img}} becomes quadratic in each block when the other is held fixed. BCD alternates between an 𝐋\mathbf{L}-step and a Δ​𝐏\Delta\mathbf{P}-step, each treating the other block as constant. Concretely, the pixel constraint 𝐂′​(𝐱n)=𝐜ntgt\mathbf{C}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{n})=\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}} (Eq. 8) rearranges to (𝐜ntgt−𝐂0​(𝐱n))=∑i=1KWi​(𝐱n)​Δ​𝐩i+δ⁡(𝐱n)⋅𝟙\big(\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}}-\mathbf{C}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{K}W_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}+\delta(\mathbf{x}_{n})\cdot\mathbb{1}, splitting the color residual between palette and luminance contributions. The 𝐋\mathbf{L}-step absorbs the luminance residual that Δ​𝐏\Delta\mathbf{P} has not covered (projecting onto 𝐰L\mathbf{w}_{L} (International Telecommunication Union, 2015)),

(14) Δ​L∗​(𝐱n)=𝐰L⊤​(𝐜ntgt−𝐂0​(𝐱n))−𝐰L⊤​∑i=1KWi​(𝐱n)​Δ​𝐩i,\Delta L^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\;=\;\mathbf{w}_{L}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}}-\mathbf{C}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\big)\;-\;\mathbf{w}_{L}^{\top}\!\!\sum_{i=1}^{K}W_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i},

while the Δ​𝐏\Delta\mathbf{P}-step absorbs the full color residual that δ\delta has not covered,

(15) 𝐫P​(𝐱n)=(𝐜ntgt−𝐂0​(𝐱n))−δ⁡(𝐱n)⋅𝟙.\mathbf{r}^{P}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\;=\;\big(\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\mathrm{tgt}}-\mathbf{C}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\big)\;-\;\delta(\mathbf{x}_{n})\cdot\mathbb{1}.

The asymmetry is intentional: δ\delta acts only along the grey axis, so projecting onto luminance (Eq. 14) determines its target; Δ​𝐏\Delta\mathbf{P} acts in 3D, so it must see the full residual (Eq. 15) including the grey-axis component, otherwise the chromatic palette shifts cannot absorb luminance work and δ\delta alone bears it. This distinguishes our setup from Chao et al. (2023a), whose Lab-space residual decomposes orthogonally so that each block sees an independent projection. Combining IRLS with BCD yields three cheap sub-problems: an 𝐋\mathbf{L}-step that solves a sparse linear system in S​KSK unknowns, a Δ​𝐏\Delta\mathbf{P}-step that solves a small unconstrained quadratic in 3​(K−2)3(K-2) unknowns via inner IRLS, and a closed-form dd-step from the variational identity. Plain alternation oscillates because both blocks satisfy the grey-axis component of the image-space residual: tone curves contribute δ⁡(𝐱)⋅𝟙\delta(\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbb{1}, chromatic palette shifts contribute the grey-axis projection of ∑iWi​(𝐱)​Δ​𝐩i\sum_{i}W_{i}(\mathbf{x})\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}, and each block’s update absorbs whatever the other just provided. We damp each block update with a convex combination of the previous iterate, breaking the oscillation and yielding monotone convergence in practice. Convergence typically requires 5–15 outer iterations and tens of milliseconds per edit; explicit forms of the 𝐋\mathbf{L} and Δ​𝐏\Delta\mathbf{P} systems, the damping rule, and the full algorithm are provided in the supplemental.

6. Results and Evaluation

We demonstrate a range of editing capabilities: palette-based recoloring (Figs. 1, 3, 5, 7, 8), palette-aware luminance editing (Figs. 1, 2, 3, 7, 8), and pixel-level color constraints (Figs. 1, 8); see the supplemental for more results. All edits run in real-time, propagate consistently across novel views, and can bake back into vanilla 3DGS for use with standard viewers.

6.1. Implementation Details and Performance

We implement our method in PyTorch with custom CUDA kernels for efficient weight splatting, and the real-time editing interface in Rust on top of Brush (Brussee, 2024), a WebGPU-based 3DGS viewer. The interface sustains ∼200{\sim}200 FPS on a MacBook Pro with Apple Silicon (M5 Pro, 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU, 24 GB unified memory). Across all examples, we finetune with weight SH of degree L=3L=3, the rank-1 factorization of §4.4 for higher-order SH, and K=5K=5 or 66 palette colors. Each scene is finetuned for 30–50 epochs from a pretrained vanilla 3DGS checkpoint using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) with views shuffled per epoch, taking 40 s to 3 min on NVIDIA H200 (Table 1). Chromatic palette vertices {𝐩i}i=3K\{\mathbf{p}_{i}\}_{i=3}^{K} are initialized from a simplified convex hull (Tan et al., 2016) of the frozen renders with quantization; black and white are fixed. Hyperparameters: λpos=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{pos}}=0.5, λcompact=0.001\lambda_{\mathrm{compact}}=0.001 (ramped 5×5\times after the first 2/32/3 of training), λsep=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}}=1.0 with minimum hue-gap fraction 0.30.3 (§4.3). For transparent-background scenes, we add an alpha-channel supervision term (λalpha=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{alpha}}=1.0). After 70%70\% of training we clamp barycentric supervision targets to the simplex to prevent negative splatted weights (which would invert palette edits at those pixels). We follow the evaluation protocol of Barron et al. (2021): hold out every 8th image as a test view, and train vanilla 3DGS baselines with uniform default settings across all scenes. At edit time, the constraint-driven solver (§5.2) runs on a single CPU thread and converges in  8 outer iterations of damped BCD (α=0.7\alpha=0.7). All edits complete in 5–15 ms.

6.2. Evaluation

We evaluate on three aspects: reconstruction fidelity to verify that editability does not degrade too much on novel-view synthesis (Table 1); edit locality and consistency under palette and tone-curve modifications (Fig. 9); and pixel-level editing against primitive-space baselines. The supplemental presents additional evaluations and comparisons (§E), a proof of lossless palette bake-back together with finetuning time and quality for tone-curve bake-back (§B), and an extensive investigation of a Lab-space variant (§D, closer to Chao et al. (2023a)) that splats palette weights and lightness as separate SH-encoded quantities and edits in CIELAB ab-space, which informed our choice of RGB by exposing two structural drawbacks: a non-linear Lab-to-RGB transform at edit time and the loss of closed-form palette bake-back.

We compare against our implementations of recent palette-based 3DGS methods 33 3 Code is available at https://github.com/tedchao/ReparamGS-Palette/tree/main/others, PaletteGaussian (Ren et al., 2024) and RecolorGaussian (Bi et al., 2025), both of which decompose appearance in primitive space (per Gaussian). Despite per-Gaussian sparsity regularization, alpha blending during rasterization mixes contributions from many Gaussians at each pixel, so pixel weights are non-sparse in view-space and palette edits bleed into unintended regions (Fig. 9 and supplemental §E.2). For pixel-level editing (§E.3), the primitive-space baselines require joint gradient descent over palette and per-Gaussian SH, taking 3.75–13.02 s per edit on NVIDIA H200 while still exhibiting color bleeding; over-regularizing the palette pushes the optimizer to compensate through the view-dependent SH originally intended for specular effects, producing an unnatural appearance (Fig. 6 in supplemental). We additionally compare against a 2D editing heuristic that edits a single rendered view with ColorfulCurves (Chao et al., 2023a) and finetunes the per-Gaussian SH to reproduce the edit (§E.1). Because supervision is available only on the edited view, the heuristic produces visible artifacts in novel views and adds 5.25.2 s of SH finetuning per edit. In contrast, our view-space formulation achieves localized edits through a constraint-driven solve over the palette 𝐏\mathbf{P} and tone curves {fi}\{f_{i}\} alone, with all Gaussian parameters fixed, propagating consistently across novel views. PaletteGaussian additionally proposes object-level editing through a second-stage training pass with segmentation masks. The masks shown in their work are coarse and lack the soft boundaries needed for natural color compositing in complex regions such as forests, as noted by Chao et al. (2023a). More critically, even when segmentation succeeds, the underlying primitive-space weights are still non-sparse after alpha blending, so the same locality limitations and color bleeding persist within each segmented region.

7. Conclusion

Palette-based image editing follows a simple recipe: take an image, reparametrize it for editability. We present a real-time color grading approach for 3D Gaussian Splatting that applies the same principle in 3D. Our method reparametrizes a pretrained vanilla 3DGS into a view-space palette decomposition, in which each Gaussian carries weight SH that alpha-blend into per-pixel mixing weights over a small, scene-adaptive palette. We supervise the reparametrization with differentiable barycentric targets to obtain sparse, color-consistent weights, and we encode the higher-order weight SH with a rank-1 factorization that roughly halves the storage of vanilla 3DGS. We design a constraint-driven solver based on dBCD with IRLS that jointly satisfies palette, tone-curve, and pixel-level color constraints in tens of milliseconds per edit, and the edited representation bakes back into a vanilla 3DGS: palette edits in closed-form, tone-curve edits in seconds of finetuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across a variety of scenes and editing scenarios.

Limitations and Future Work.

Our method has several limitations that suggest directions for future work. First, our representation requires a brief finetuning stage from a pretrained vanilla 3DGS; deriving an analytical mapping from color SH to weight SH given a palette would remove this stage entirely. Second, tone-curve edits cannot be baked back in closed-form because the per-pixel luminance shift is non-linear in the rendered color, so they require a brief finetuning stage. Reducing or eliminating this stage, for instance by approximating the luminance shift with a piecewise-linear correction baked into the weight SH, is an interesting direction. Third, our method does not support semantic or object-level editing constraints. Incorporating segmentation-aware decompositions (Chao et al., 2023b; Aksoy et al., 2018), as demonstrated for NeRFs (Chen et al., 2025), could enable selective recoloring of specific objects or materials while preserving our view-space sparsity advantages.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
